questions.prompt: In C++23, what does the standard require of a compiler translating `demo`?
options: It must reject the program: discarding the result is ill-formed
It must issue a diagnostic, but may still accept the program
Nothing: a warning is only recommended practice
Nothing, but calling `demo` is undefined behavior
questions.explanation: [dcl.attr.nodiscard] only encourages a warning when a nodiscard call's result is discarded; it appears under recommended practice. The program is well-formed, a silent compiler is conforming, and nothing about the call's behavior changes. GCC and Clang do warn, which is why the first two options feel right.

questions.prompt: In C++23, is this program well-formed? No compiler you know of supports `acme::fast`.
options: Ill-formed: `acme::fast` is not a recognized attribute
Well-formed: an unrecognized attribute is ignored
Implementation-defined behavior
Ill-formed: attribute namespaces other than `gnu`, `clang` and `msvc` are reserved
questions.explanation: Since C++17, [dcl.attr.grammar] says an attribute token the implementation does not recognize is ignored, which is what lets vendor attributes appear in portable code. Compilers usually warn, as GCC does with `-Wattributes`. Implementation-defined behavior was the C++11 and C++14 rule for attributes not specified by the standard.

questions.prompt: In C++23, what does this program print?
options: Undefined behavior
Nothing: an assumption may not have side effects, so it is ill-formed
questions.explanation: The expression of an assumption is never evaluated, so `++i` never runs and `i` is still 0. There is no undefined behavior, because the expression would be true if it were evaluated. Side effects are allowed in the expression; they are simply discarded, and Clang warns that such an assumption is ignored.

questions.prompt: In C++23, what is the effect of this declaration?
options: `Error` becomes a nodiscard type, the same as `struct [[nodiscard]] Error`
The attribute is ignored because it is in an unrecognized position
It is ill-formed: an attribute at the start of a declaration needs a declarator to appertain to
The attribute applies to the next function declared
questions.explanation: An attribute specifier at the start of a simple declaration appertains to the entities its declarators declare, and the grammar only allows it when there is a declarator list. This declaration has none, so it is ill-formed; the class attribute belongs after the class key, as in `struct [[nodiscard]] Error`. Clang rejects it, while GCC only warns that the attribute is ignored, which makes the second option look right.

questions.prompt: Which of the discarded calls in `demo` are nodiscard calls, the ones compilers are encouraged to warn about?
options: Both calls
Only `make()`
Only `last()`
Neither: the attribute is on the type, not on the functions
questions.explanation: A nodiscard call is a call to a function declared nodiscard, or a call whose return type is a class or enumeration type marked nodiscard. `make` returns `Error` by value, so it qualifies. `last` returns `Error&`, a reference type, so the type's attribute does not apply; GCC warns about `make()` only.

questions.prompt: In C++23, is this function well-formed?
options: Well-formed: falling out of the switch is a kind of fall-through
Undefined behavior only when the default branch is taken
Well-formed, but compilers may warn
Ill-formed: the second `[[fallthrough]];` is not followed by a case or default label
questions.explanation: [dcl.attr.fallthrough] requires the next statement executed after a fallthrough statement to be labelled with a case or default label of the same switch, and makes the program ill-formed if there is no such statement. The first use is fine; the second sits at the end of the switch. Clang rejects it, while GCC only warns, which is a permitted diagnostic but makes the third option tempting.

questions.prompt: In C++23, is this translation unit well-formed?
options: Ill-formed: the first declaration must specify `noreturn` if any declaration does
Well-formed: attributes accumulate across redeclarations
Ill-formed, no diagnostic required
Well-formed, and undefined behavior only if `stop` returns
questions.explanation: [dcl.attr.noreturn] says the first declaration of a function shall specify `noreturn` if any of its declarations does. Within one translation unit that is an ordinary diagnosable rule, and both GCC and Clang reject this. The no-diagnostic-required case is the cross-file one, where a function is declared `noreturn` in one translation unit and without it in another. Many other attributes, such as `deprecated`, may be added on a redeclaration, which is why the second option is tempting.

questions.prompt: For an object `p` of type `Pair`, which of these does the C++23 standard guarantee?
options: `sizeof(Pair) == sizeof(int)`
`(void*)&p.a == (void*)&p.b`
`(void*)&p.a != (void*)&p.b`
`sizeof(Pair) > sizeof(int)`
questions.explanation: [intro.object] allows two objects with overlapping lifetimes to share an address only if one is nested in the other, or at least one is a zero-size subobject and their types are not similar. `a` and `b` have the same type, so their addresses must differ even though both may be zero-size. Neither size claim is guaranteed: the attribute only permits overlap, and MSVC ignores it entirely.
